chapter_theme: The inability to bear parting. Mostly in the woman's voice, the chapter argues against his leaving before it happens: promises of a quick return are useless to one who won't survive, and a broken 'fear not' makes trust itself hard.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's headnotes run from the man announcing departure (1151) to her sensing it (1152-1155), hearing of it through her friend (1156-1158), and answering the friend's advice to bear up (1159-1160).

1151.reading: If you aren't leaving, tell me; if you mean to return quickly, tell that to those who will still be alive by then; the speaker is the friend for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
1151.nuance: One of the book's sharpest lines, a refusal to accept comfort. If the friend is the speaker, then Parimelazhagar's explanation for 'me' matters: she says எனக்கு for the woman because the two aren't distinct. He notes that some give the verse to the woman.

positions.position: The friend answers the man, who has promised a quick return, and aims to stop his leaving.
positions.quote: 'பிரிந்து கடிதின் வருவல்' என்ற தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

positions.position: The woman answers the friend, who has told her he will come back soon.
positions.quote: இது கடித்து வருவாரென்ற தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் ஆற்றாமையாற் கூறி யது.

1152.reading: The woman says that பார்வல் alone once gave her delight, and now union itself holds the pain of fearing separation.
1152.nuance: The cruelty is that the most that love can give is spoiled by what it anticipates. Parimelazhagar cites Kalittokai for the telling sign: he now fusses over her more than before, which is how she knows he is leaving.

positions.position: பார்வல் is his look back in courtship, sweet because it promised union.
positions.quote: அவர் நோக்கு மாத்திரமும் புணர்ச்சி குறித்தமையான் நமக்கு இன்ப முடைத்தாயிருக்கும்

positions.position: It is her own watching for his arrival, a present joy set against the anxiety of being with him.

1153.reading: The woman says trust is hard, since parting sometimes happens even with those who understand.
1153.nuance: அறிவுடையார் isn't a compliment to his learning. Parimelazhagar's gloss is that he knows his own word and knows she can't bear it, which makes his going worse. The verse shifts from this man's fault to the general difficulty of trusting anyone.

1154.reading: The woman asks, if the one who was gracious and told her not to fear should leave, whether any fault lies with those who believed his assuring words.
1154.nuance: She refers to herself in the third person as தேறியார், 'those who trusted', which both commentators note. This turns the private complaint into a general moral question about a promise and who answers for it. Parimelazhagar names the fault as the mismatch between his word and deed.

1155.reading: The woman tells her friend that if she wants to protect her, she must prevent the departure of the one who is fit for her, because once he goes, union will be hard.
1155.nuance: அமைந்தார் is a quiet word: the one who is fitting. Parimelazhagar adds divine ordering, saying he is the one fit by தெய்வம் to be her lord, and Pope follows with 'destined'. The verse itself doesn't mention destiny. He also explains why union would be hard: her life would have gone with him.

1156.reading: The woman says that if he can be so hard as to speak of leaving, the hope that he would come back and be gracious is pointless.
1156.nuance: The offence is the announcement, even more than the journey. For Parimelazhagar, one who could plan this while still at her side isn't likely to soften at a distance.

1157.reading: The woman asks if the bangles slipping past her wrist don't already announce that the lord of the shore has left her.
1157.nuance: தூற்றா is the verb for spreading gossip, so her own body has joined the town. Parimelazhagar sees a rebuke to the friend, who brings the news: 'you too only do what these bangles do', when she should have stopped him. The past tense 'has left' is anticipatory, since the news alone has made her thin.

1158.reading: The woman says living in a town without one's own people is painful, and being parted from the one who is dear is more painful still.
1158.nuance: This sounds like a proverb, but Parimelazhagar says it is aimed. Her friend agreed to his leaving instead of preventing it, and so she speaks as if she has no companion here at all, while seeming only to speak about the way of the world.

1159.reading: Fire burns only when touched, and can it burn when one moves away, as the sickness of love does? The speaker is the woman for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.

positions.position: The woman answers the friend, who has said love burns only where it is, like fire, and that she should therefore bear it.
positions.quote: 'காமம் தீயே போன்று தான் நின்ற இடத்தைச் சுடுமாகலான் நீ ஆற்றல் வேண்டும்' என்ற தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

positions.position: The friend speaks, on seeing the woman's distress after the man has left.

1160.reading: The woman says that many agree to the impossible, remove their pain, endure the parting, and stay on alive afterwards.
1160.nuance: It is all in the tone. Taken flatly, as Pope's couplet takes it, this says many cope; read as Parimelazhagar does, 'many' means no one, and the unstated close is that she too will die. Kalaignar makes the turn explicit by adding, 'but I?'. The three verbs slow down the task of enduring.

links.note: 510 warns that trusting without examination and doubting after trust both bring endless grief, for those choosing men to work with. 1153 is that same predicament without any such procedure: there is no way to test the one she has already trusted.
Both quote 'fear not' against him. In 1149 his failure removes her shame before the town. In 1154 it raises the question of fault. One promise is doing a lot of work in her argument.
Fear of parting spoils union in 1152. By 1179 it is routine: her eyes can't sleep when he is away or when he is home. Anticipation has become a permanent condition.

source_issues: Chapter title: the source gives கற்பியல், which names the section beginning here. The chapter's own title, பிரிவாற்றாமை, is missing.

1153: Manakkudavar's entry, flagged [#], is word for word the same as Parimelazhagar's gloss, and appears to be borrowed to fill a gap. The same flag appears at 1134 and 1140 and the wording matches there too. It should not be treated as independent witness.
1158: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary, and Parimelazhagar's entry begins மதுவும் அது, an apparent typo for இதுவும் அது.
